questions.stem:
(a) Explain the following colour terms: (i) primary colours (ii) secondary colours (iii) complementary colours. [6 marks]
(b) State two ways in which an artist can create texture in a two-dimensional work. [4 marks]
(c) Describe how line can be used to express calmness and excitement in a picture. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Primary colours cannot be produced by mixing other colours; red, yellow and blue
2 marks: Secondary colours are made by mixing two primaries; orange, green, violet
2 marks: Complementary colours lie opposite on the colour wheel, e.g. red/green, blue/orange
2 marks: Visual texture by hatching, stippling or dry brush
2 marks: Actual texture by impasto, collage or adding sand/sawdust to paint
2 marks: Horizontal and gently curved lines suggest calm and rest
3 marks: Diagonal, zigzag, broken or thick jagged lines suggest movement, tension and excitement
questions.explanation: Primaries (red, yellow, blue) are basic; mixing two gives secondaries; opposites on the wheel are complements. Texture can be implied by mark-making or built up physically. Horizontal lines feel restful, while diagonals and zigzags feel energetic.

questions.stem:
(a) What is perspective in drawing? [2 marks]
(b) Distinguish between linear perspective and aerial perspective. [6 marks]
(c) Explain the following terms: (i) eye level (ii) vanishing point (iii) foreshortening. [7 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Perspective is the method of representing three-dimensional objects and depth on a flat surface
3 marks: Linear perspective uses converging lines and diminishing sizes towards vanishing points
3 marks: Aerial perspective shows distance through paler, bluer, less detailed and less contrasting forms
2 marks: Eye level is the horizontal line at the height of the viewer's eyes (horizon line)
2 marks: Vanishing point is where receding parallel lines appear to meet on the eye level
3 marks: Foreshortening is the apparent shortening of a form pointing towards or away from the viewer
questions.explanation: Perspective creates the illusion of depth. Linear perspective relies on geometry; aerial perspective relies on atmosphere and colour. Eye level, vanishing points and foreshortening are its key terms.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem:
(a) Name two ancient art cultures of Nigeria apart from Nok. [2 marks]
(b) Describe four features of Nok terracotta sculpture. [8 marks]
(c) State the importance of Nok art to the history of Nigeria. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Any one of Ife, Benin, Igbo-Ukwu
1 mark: Any other of Ife, Benin, Igbo-Ukwu, Esie, Owo, Tada/Jebba
2 marks: Made of baked clay (terracotta)
2 marks: Pierced eyes, usually triangular or D-shaped, with heavy brows
2 marks: Elaborate hairstyles and ornaments such as beads
2 marks: Large, often cylindrical heads in proportion to the body; stylised features
2 marks: Oldest known sculptural tradition in Nigeria, showing early civilisation
3 marks: Evidence of early iron working, dress, ornament and social life; source of national pride and tourism
questions.explanation: Nok terracottas, found near Nok during tin mining, show pierced eyes, elaborate hairstyles, beads and stylised heads. They are among the oldest sculptures south of the Sahara and reveal early iron-age life in Nigeria.

questions.topic: Ancient Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem:
(a) Describe the lost-wax (cire perdue) method of casting as practised by Benin brass casters. [10 marks]
(b) State five subjects represented on Benin brass plaques. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Clay core is modelled roughly to the shape of the object
2 marks: Wax is applied over the core and details are modelled and incised in the wax
2 marks: Wax is covered with fine clay and further clay layers, with channels/runners made
2 marks: Mould is heated so the wax melts and runs out, leaving a cavity
2 marks: Molten brass is poured in, cooled, the mould broken and the cast chased and polished
1 mark: The Oba and royal attendants
1 mark: Warriors and battle scenes
1 mark: Court officials and chiefs
1 mark: Portuguese traders/foreigners
1 mark: Animals such as leopards, fish or birds
questions.explanation: A clay core is covered in wax worked to fine detail, then sealed in clay with runners. Heating removes the wax; molten brass fills the space; the mould is broken and the cast finished. Plaques show the Oba, warriors, chiefs, Portuguese visitors and symbolic animals.

questions.topic: Modern Traditional Art of West Africa
questions.stem:
(a) Explain the term modern traditional art. [3 marks]
(b) Describe the making of adire eleko. [8 marks]
(c) Name two other traditional textiles in Nigeria and the people associated with each. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Traditional art still produced today by indigenous artists using inherited methods and serving local needs
2 marks: White cotton cloth is spread and cassava starch paste (eko) prepared
2 marks: Paste is applied with a feather, stick or through a zinc stencil to form designs
2 marks: Cloth is dried and dipped repeatedly in indigo dye
2 marks: Paste is scraped off and the cloth washed to reveal white patterns on blue
2 marks: One correct textile and people, e.g. aso oke (Yoruba)
2 marks: Another correct one, e.g. akwete (Igbo), tie-dye/tiv cloth (Tiv), Bida cloth (Nupe)
questions.explanation: Modern traditional art continues inherited forms today. In adire eleko, starch paste resists the indigo; when scraped off, white designs remain. Other examples are aso oke and akwete.

questions.stem: Write short notes on any three of the following artists, stating for each one their main medium and one notable contribution: (a) Ben Enwonwu (b) Bruce Onobrakpeya (c) Uche Okeke (d) Lamidi Fakeye (e) El Anatsui. [15 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: First artist: correct medium (2), contribution or work (3)
5 marks: Second artist: correct medium (2), contribution or work (3)
5 marks: Third artist: correct medium (2), contribution or work (3)
questions.explanation: Enwonwu: painter and sculptor, Anyanwu. Onobrakpeya: printmaker, plastocast and the Harmattan Workshop. Okeke: painter, Uli revival and natural synthesis. Fakeye: Yoruba woodcarver of doors and posts. El Anatsui: sculptor, metal bottle-cap hangings.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain three conventions observed by ancient Egyptian painters in representing the human figure. [9 marks]
(b) Give two reasons why the Egyptians decorated tombs. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Law of frontality: head and legs in profile, eye and shoulders frontal
3 marks: Hierarchical scale: important people drawn larger
3 marks: Canon of proportion based on a grid; figures arranged in registers/bands
3 marks: Belief in the afterlife: images provided for the dead in the next world
3 marks: Record the life, status and deeds of the deceased
questions.explanation: Egyptian figures combined profile and frontal views, ranked size by importance and followed a grid-based canon. Tomb art served the dead in the afterlife and recorded their status.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the three orders of Greek architecture. [9 marks]
(b) Mention two features that distinguish Classical Greek sculpture from Archaic sculpture. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Doric: plain cushion-like capital, no base, sturdy fluted column
3 marks: Ionic: scroll (volute) capital, slender column with base
3 marks: Corinthian: ornate capital with acanthus leaves, slender with base
3 marks: Classical figures use contrapposto and natural relaxed poses; archaic figures are stiff and frontal
3 marks: Classical faces are calm and idealised; archaic faces show the fixed archaic smile
questions.explanation: Doric is plain and sturdy; Ionic has scroll capitals; Corinthian has acanthus leaves. Classical sculpture moved from stiff archaic poses with fixed smiles to natural contrapposto and idealised calm.

questions.stem:
(a) What was the Renaissance? [3 marks]
(b) State four characteristics of Italian Renaissance art. [8 marks]
(c) Name two Renaissance artists and one work by each. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Rebirth of classical learning and art in Europe, beginning in Italy in the 14th-15th centuries
2 marks: Use of linear perspective
2 marks: Realistic anatomy and proportion based on study
2 marks: Chiaroscuro / sfumato modelling
2 marks: Revival of classical Greek and Roman themes and humanism
2 marks: First artist and work, e.g. Leonardo, The Last Supper
2 marks: Second artist and work, e.g. Michelangelo, David
questions.explanation: The Renaissance revived classical ideals. Artists used perspective, anatomy and light and shade. Examples: Leonardo (Last Supper, Mona Lisa), Michelangelo (David), Raphael (School of Athens).

questions.stem:
(a) Explain how Post-Impressionism differed from Impressionism. [5 marks]
(b) Discuss the contribution of any two of the following: Paul Cézanne, Vincent van Gogh, Paul Gauguin, Georges Seurat. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Post-Impressionists kept bright colour but rejected mere recording of light
2 marks: They emphasised structure, symbolism or personal emotion
5 marks: First artist: style and contribution, e.g. Cézanne reduced nature to geometric forms, influencing Cubism
5 marks: Second artist: style and contribution, e.g. Van Gogh's expressive brushwork; Gauguin's flat colour; Seurat's pointillism
questions.explanation: Post-Impressionists went beyond fleeting light: Cézanne built solid geometric structure, Van Gogh expressed emotion in swirling strokes, Gauguin used flat symbolic colour and Seurat applied scientific dots.
